title: Logic and fallacies
examples: What is the difference between a fallacy and a weak argument?
Can you give me an example of a valid argument in everyday life?
How do I spot a straw man fallacy when I am reading?

explain.say: Today we are learning about how to spot weak arguments.

items: Arguments must have a clear conclusion.

explain.say: A valid argument means the conclusion must follow the premises.
The straw man fallacy happens when someone misrepresents an argument.
Ad hominem attacks the person instead of their actual argument.
The slippery slope suggests a small step leads to huge problems.

items: Step 1: Lowering the speed limit by five miles per hour
Step 2: Next, they will ban cars entirely
Step 3: Eventually, we will all walk everywhere

draw.text: Slippery Slope: Small step to big problem

explain.say: In real life, consider a debate about school uniforms.

faq.q: What is the difference between a weak argument and a fallacy?
faq.a: A weak argument simply lacks good evidence to support its claim. A fallacy is a specific flaw in the structure of the reasoning itself.
asks: Is a weak argument always a fallacy?
What makes an argument structurally flawed?

faq.q: How do I know if an argument is valid?
faq.a: You check if the conclusion absolutely must be true if you accept the starting statements as true. If it must be true, the argument is valid.
asks: Does the conclusion have to follow the premises?
What is the test for valid logic?

faq.q: When is the straw man fallacy most common?
faq.a: It is very common in heated debates or political discussions. People often twist what others say to make it easier to attack.
asks: How can I spot a misrepresentation of an idea?

faq.q: Does ad hominem always mean personal insults?
faq.a: No, it means attacking the source of the argument rather than the argument itself. It can be subtle, like questioning someone's motives.
asks: Is criticizing the person the same as attacking the argument?
What if I question their credibility?

faq.q: Is the slippery slope fallacy always exaggerated?
faq.a: Yes, it exaggerates the connection between a small initial action and a massive, inevitable outcome. It skips necessary steps.
asks: Does a small change always lead to disaster?
How many steps must I prove for a slope to be real?

facts: A valid argument structure guarantees that if the premises are true, the conclusion must also be true.
The straw man fallacy involves replacing an opponent's actual argument with a weaker, distorted version.
Ad hominem attacks are fallacious because they ignore the logical content of the statement.
The slippery slope fallacy assumes a chain of events will happen without providing evidence for each link.

quiz.say: Premise 1: All dogs have fur. Premise 2: Fluffy has fur. Conclusion: Therefore, Fluffy is a dog.
quiz.why: The conclusion does not necessarily follow from the premises; other things besides dogs can have fur.

wrong.1: This is tempting because the premises sound true, but the conclusion is not guaranteed.
wrong.2: This is wrong because the argument is not misrepresenting anyone else's point.
wrong.3: This is wrong because the argument does not attack a person's character.

quiz.say: A politician says, 'You only support this bill because you received money from the company.'
quiz.why: This attacks the supporter's motives instead of discussing the bill's merits.

wrong.0: This is wrong because the politician is not twisting a previous argument.
wrong.1: This is wrong because it does not predict a chain of future events.
wrong.2: This is wrong because the argument's structure is flawed by attacking the person.

quiz.say: If we allow students to wear hoodies to school, soon they will skip class entirely, and then they will never learn anything.
quiz.why: This suggests a chain of events without proving each step must happen.

wrong.0: This is wrong because it does not attack a specific person.
wrong.1: This is wrong because it is not misrepresenting a single, clear argument.
wrong.2: This is wrong because the connection between the steps is not logically proven.
